title: Binary Heap Fundamentals
summary: A binary heap is a complete binary tree packed into a flat array, giving O(1) peek at the min or max and O(log n) insert/remove without ever storing an explicit tree.

slides.markdown:
A **binary heap** is the structure behind every priority queue: a scheduler picking the next task, Dijkstra's algorithm picking the next closest node, `heapq` in Python or `PriorityQueue` in Java.

The trick is deceptively simple — store a complete binary tree **in a flat array**, no pointers at all, and enforce one weak ordering rule: every parent is smaller (or larger) than its children.

That single rule buys O(1) access to the minimum (or maximum) and O(log n) insert and remove — cheaper than keeping the whole collection sorted, and simpler than balancing a search tree.

slides.subTitle: Min-heap and max-heap
slides.markdown:
The **heap property** is one rule applied at every node: in a **min-heap**, each parent's value is ≤ both its children's values; in a **max-heap**, each parent's value is ≥ both children.

That is strictly weaker than a binary search tree's ordering. A BST guarantees a full left-to-right sorted order via in-order traversal. A heap guarantees only a **vertical** relationship — parent versus its own children. Two sibling subtrees have **no defined relationship** to each other at all.

What you give up (full ordering) buys what you actually need for a priority queue: fast access to *one* extreme value, not a sorted view of everything.

slides.subTitle: Parent and child index formulas
slides.markdown:
A binary heap never allocates a node or a pointer. It stores values in a plain array and reconstructs the tree shape from **index arithmetic** alone (0-indexed):

```text
parent(i) = (i - 1) // 2
leftChild(i)  = 2*i + 1
rightChild(i) = 2*i + 2
```

Walking the array left to right and laying nodes level by level reproduces the tree exactly, because the tree is **complete** (next section) — there are never gaps to skip over. This is why heaps are so cheap in practice: no per-node memory overhead, and every step is one array index computation instead of a pointer dereference.

slides.subTitle: Trading full ordering for simplicity
slides.markdown:
Both structures organize data hierarchically, but for very different jobs:

| | Binary heap | Balanced BST |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering guarantee | parent vs. own children only | full left < node < right, everywhere |
| Find the min/max | O(1) peek at the root | O(log n) walk to a leaf |
| Search arbitrary value | O(n) — no help from the property | O(log n) |
| Storage | flat array, no pointers | nodes + left/right pointers |
| Rebalancing | none needed — always complete | rotations required (AVL/red-black) |

Reach for a heap when the only question you ever ask is **"what's the current min/max?"** — a task scheduler, an event queue, a top-K stream. Reach for a BST when you need **ordered traversal or arbitrary lookups**, like a sorted map. Using a BST just to repeatedly pop the minimum is strictly more machinery than the job needs.

The single most common heap mistake: reading the backing array left to right and expecting sorted order.

A valid min-heap array might be `[1, 3, 2, 7, 6, 5, 4]`. Index 3 (value 7) and index 4 (value 6) are siblings under index 1 (value 3) — nothing says 7 must come before 6, or that either must be less than index 2's subtree. The **only** guarantee that array satisfies is: every `arr[i] <= arr[2i+1]` and `arr[i] <= arr[2i+2]`.

If you need the fully sorted sequence, you have to actually **extract** repeatedly (that's heap sort, covered next topic) — the raw array is not a shortcut to it. Print a heap's array in an interview and someone will assume it's sorted; it never is, past the root.

A **complete binary tree** fills every level fully except possibly the last, which fills strictly left to right with no gaps. A heap is *always* kept complete — that's not a side detail, it's what makes the array trick legal.

Without completeness, the index formulas from earlier would break: `2*i + 1` would sometimes point at a slot that doesn't correspond to a real node, and you'd need explicit null markers or pointers to skip the gaps — exactly the overhead the array representation exists to avoid.

Completeness also caps the height at **⌊log₂ n⌋**, which is the real reason heap operations are O(log n): every insert or removal only ever has to travel up or down one root-to-leaf path, and that path is never longer than log₂ n.

Completeness makes a heap's height grow astonishingly slowly, which is worth internalizing with real sizes:

- 1,000 elements → height ≈ ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ = **9**
- 1,000,000 elements → height ≈ **19**
- 1,000,000,000 elements → height ≈ **29**

A thousand-fold increase in size costs only about 10 extra levels. That's why a priority queue backing a task scheduler with millions of pending jobs still does insert/extract in a few dozen comparisons — the tree never gets tall, because it can't: completeness forces it to grow *wide* first, one full level at a time, instead of stretching deep and lopsided the way an unbalanced BST can.

slides.subTitle: Root-is-min vs. every-level-is-sorted
slides.markdown:
A related but distinct mistake from "the array is sorted": assuming that because the **root** is the minimum, **every level** must be sorted, or that a parent's left child is always ≤ its right child.

Neither is guaranteed. The heap property only constrains a node against its *own* two children — it says nothing about comparing one subtree to a sibling subtree, and nothing about left-versus-right ordering between two children of the same parent. A left child can be larger than its right sibling; a node deep in one subtree can be smaller than a node much higher up in a different subtree, as long as it's still larger than its own ancestors.

The only fact you can rely on, always: **root ≤ everything** (min-heap) or **root ≥ everything** (max-heap). Nothing below the root is comparable to anything outside its own direct ancestor chain.

Binary heaps are not a textbook curiosity — they're load-bearing in real systems:

- **OS and thread schedulers** use a priority heap to pick the next runnable task by priority/deadline.
- **Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms** use a min-heap to always expand the closest unvisited node next.
- **`epoll`/timer wheels and event loops** use heaps to fire the soonest-expiring timer first.
- **Huffman coding** repeatedly merges the two lowest-frequency nodes — exactly a min-heap's extract-extract-insert pattern.
- **Merge-K-sorted-streams** (log compaction, external sort merge phase) uses a heap seeded with one element per stream.

The common thread: whenever "give me the current best/next candidate, then let a new candidate arrive" repeats in a loop, a heap is almost always the right tool, and later topics in this group walk through several of these patterns directly.

You *could* implement a heap with explicit `Node` objects and `left`/`right` pointers, the way a BST is usually built. Almost nobody does, for good reason:

| | Array-backed heap | Pointer-based tree heap |
|---|---|---|
| Memory per element | just the value | value + 2–3 pointers |
| Cache behavior | contiguous, cache-friendly | scattered, pointer-chasing |
| Finding parent/child | O(1) arithmetic | requires stored parent pointer or search |
| Resizing | dynamic array (amortized O(1) append) | trivial (just allocate a node) |

The array form wins on every practical axis for a *complete* tree, which is precisely why every mainstream language's built-in priority queue (`heapq`, `PriorityQueue`, `std::priority_queue`) is array-backed under the hood.

You now have the shape and the rule. What's left is the *mechanism*: how an element that violates the heap property on insert gets moved back into place (**sift-up**), how removing the root gets patched (**sift-down**), and how an entire array gets turned into a valid heap in linear time (**build-heap**) rather than one slow insert at a time.

The next topic, Heap Operations: Insert, Extract, and Build-Heap, builds all three from the same two primitives.
